relation: Definition and design element: time pressure and low task experience (board members in a 10-minute briefing) are named mediators; our flags are worded as verdicts ("Architecture likely wrong"), the recommendation form the review links to more bias. ref: Goddard, K., Roudsari, A., & Wyatt, J. C. (2012). Automation bias: A systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators. *Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association*, *19*(1), 121–127. https://doi.org/10.1136/amiajnl-2011-000089

subtheme: D. AI credibility flags, and flags that are wrong
type: other HCI (published in a general science journal)
relation: Sub-theme D; direct support for H1 with wrong flags, which is our manipulation. Our study adds a human target who can rebut the wrong flag (H2, H3).
ref: Horne, B. D., & Nevo, D. (2025). People adhere to content warning labels even when they are wrong due to ecologically rational adaptations. *Scientific Reports*, *15*(1), Article 13896. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-98221-7

subtheme: Sub-theme B: Automation bias and wrong AI advice
relation: Automation bias against context; H1 and H4: the closest finding to our "right by the textbook, wrong in context" flags. The third party who pays in our study is the CISO, whose trust is measured.
ref: Klingbeil, A., Grützner, C., & Schreck, P. (2024). Trust and reliance on AI: An experimental study on the extent and costs of overreliance on AI. *Computers in Human Behavior*, *160*, Article 108352. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2024.108352

subtheme: F. AI as challenger or second opinion in groups, and power
type: SIGCHI (CHI workshop paper; earlier system paper: Lee, S., Kim, M., Hwang, S., Kim, D., & Lee, K. (2025). Amplifying minority voices: AI-mediated devil's advocate system for inclusive group decision-making. In *Companion Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces* (pp. 17–21). https://doi.org/10.1145/3708557.3716334)
relation: Sub-theme F; context for power asymmetry. In our study the lower-expertise but higher-power party (board member) uses the AI to challenge the expert; this paper is one of the few HCI works on AI challengers in hierarchies. Preliminary, workshop-level evidence only.
ref: Lee, S., & Lee, K. (2026). Rethinking AI-mediated minority support in power-imbalanced group decision-making: From anonymity to authenticity [Position paper, CHI 2026 Workshop on Restoring Human Authenticity in AI-Mediated Communication]. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.22319

subtheme: A. Definition and dimensions of trust
relation: Definition; theme anchor for the trust measure and for the optional competence, benevolence and integrity ratings. The phrase "irrespective of the ability to monitor or control" makes the checker interesting: the checker is exactly such a monitoring device, so our study asks what happens to trust when the board member gains a way to check. Our study measures a trustor's trust in an expert in real time across flags and answers, where the model describes a slow, feedback-driven process.
ref: Mayer, R. C., Davis, J. H., & Schoorman, F. D. (1995). An integrative model of organizational trust. *Academy of Management Review*, *20*(3), 709–734. https://doi.org/10.2307/258792

subtheme: Sub-theme B: Automation bias and wrong AI advice
relation: Definition of automation bias; H1 (a wrong flag is followed) and H4 (checker participants act on the flag by questioning). Our participants are not operators supervising automation: the automation's target is another person, and the commission error is a loss of trust in that person.
ref: Parasuraman, R., & Manzey, D. H. (2010). Complacency and bias in human use of automation: An attentional integration. *Human Factors*, *52*(3), 381–410. https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055

subtheme: D. Reliability of vision-language models and LLM fact-checkers
relation: Checker reliability, as the evidence behind the brief's request. LLM checkers lean towards calling statements false, especially without context, which is the condition of a camera-only checker. A true statement from the CISO is therefore at real risk of being flagged.
ref: Quelle, D., & Bovet, A. (2024). The perils and promises of fact-checking with large language models. *Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence*, *7*, Article 1341697. https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2024.1341697

subtheme: E. The checked party's response and behaviour
relation: Response to a check; bears on H2 and H3 from the other side: a counter-message without evidence undoes only part of a correction. Suggests the CISO's bare denial may recover little trust after a flag. Here the challenger is a third party and the fact-check is correct.
ref: Stedtnitz, C., Bartle, J., & Johns, R. (2026). *Testing the resilience of fact checks against rhetorical challenge* [Preprint]. Research Square. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-7755367/v1

subtheme: B. What a fact-check does to evaluation of the checked speaker
relation: Speaker evaluation; the classic "beliefs change, support does not" result, a counter-result to H1. Our speaker is a professional expert judged by a board member, not a partisan figure judged by supporters.
ref: Swire, B., Berinsky, A. J., Lewandowsky, S., & Ecker, U. K. H. (2017). Processing political misinformation: Comprehending the Trump phenomenon. *Royal Society Open Science*, *4*(3), 160802. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.160802

subtheme: B. What a fact-check does to evaluation of the checked speaker
relation: Speaker evaluation; H1 counter-result and the "ratio" boundary. Feeling thermometers stand in for trust here, which is a weaker outcome than our trust ratings.
ref: Swire-Thompson, B., Ecker, U. K. H., Lewandowsky, S., & Berinsky, A. J. (2020). They might be a liar but they're my liar: Source evaluation and the prevalence of misinformation. *Political Psychology*, *41*(1), 21–34. https://doi.org/10.1111/pops.12586

subtheme: E. Continued influence, innuendo and belief echoes
relation: H3 and H4; a CISO who flatly denies a flag stakes high confidence, so if the participant believes the checker, the denial should cost more than a hedged answer. It also suggests the AI checker's own confident wording ("Numbers do not add up") could cost the checker credibility if the participant sees it fail. Our study does not show the participant which side is right.
ref: Tenney, E. R., MacCoun, R. J., Spellman, B. A., & Hastie, R. (2007). Calibration trumps confidence as a basis for witness credibility. *Psychological Science*, *18*(1), 46–50. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01847.x

subtheme: E. Continued influence, innuendo and belief echoes
relation: H2 counter-result; predicts that even a convincing CISO answer will not bring trust fully back to the start, because the flag leaves an echo. This is the main reason to expect H2's "above the start" to fail. Our correction comes from the accused expert, not from a neutral fact-checker, and our misinformation comes from an AI tool the participant chose to use.
ref: Thorson, E. (2016). Belief echoes: The persistent effects of corrected misinformation. *Political Communication*, *33*(3), 460–480. https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2015.1102187

subtheme: B. Industry and trade sources
relation: Context and gap. Regulation now requires boards to oversee cyber risk and assumes they will do it without subject expertise. This sets up the non-expert overseer in our scenario. Lowry et al. (2026) suggest that such oversight tends to be symbolic.
ref: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. (2023). *Cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incident disclosure* (Release Nos. 33-11216; 34-97989). https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/final/2023/33-11216.pdf

subtheme: D. AI-labelled checkers and how a checked human is judged
relation: AI versus human checker; the defended party (the outlet) gains little from an AI label. Supports a design note that an explanation of the checker's process may matter more than its being AI. Our checker attacks rather than defends.
ref: Wang, R., & Ophir, Y. (2026). Can professional or AI fact-checking protect trust in journalism from political attacks? The complex roles of source, transparency, ideology, and the machine heuristic. *Computers in Human Behavior*, *176*, 108872. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2025.108872

subtheme: Sub-theme A: Algorithm versus human advisor, and advice conflict (judge-advisor systems)
relation: Advice conflict; counter-result for H1: when a human expert and an algorithm sit side by side, judges have leaned toward the human. Our design puts them in direct conflict on the same claim, and the human is also the target of the algorithm's flag, which these studies never tested.
ref: Önkal, D., Goodwin, P., Thomson, M., Gönül, S., & Pollock, A. (2009). The relative influence of advice from human experts and statistical methods on forecast adjustments. *Journal of Behavioral Decision Making*, *22*(4), 390–409. https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.637

subtheme: D. AI-labelled checkers and how a checked human is judged
relation: AI checker credibility; design element: whether we state the checker's accuracy will change how far participants follow its flags (H4). Our participants have no prior stake in the CISO's claims, so motivated reasoning should be weaker.
ref: Amaddio, K. M., Goebel, J. T., Clark, J. K., Wegener, D. T., Garrett, R. K., Susmann, M. W., & Parthasarathy, S. (2026). Prior beliefs & automated fact checking: Limits on the effectiveness of AI-based corrections. *PLOS ONE*, *21*(2), e0342332. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342332

subtheme: C. Products: camera assistants, meeting assistants and live fact-checkers
short: Camera-based "look and ask" assistants: Ray-Ban Meta with Meta AI (2024)
relation: Product context and ecological validity of the simulated checker. Our study asks what happens when the listener uses such a tool on a human presenter, which no vendor or study has measured.
ref: Camera-based "look and ask" assistants: Ray-Ban Meta with Meta AI (2024), Apple Visual Intelligence (2024), ChatGPT Advanced Voice with video (2024), Google Gemini Live with camera (2025)

subtheme: F. AI as challenger or second opinion in groups, and power
relation: Sub-theme F; design element (an LLM that objects in a group setting). Our checker objects to a human presenter instead of to an AI, and we measure trust in that human.
ref: Chiang, C.-W., Lu, Z., Li, Z., & Yin, M. (2024). Enhancing AI-assisted group decision making through LLM-powered devil's advocate. In *Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces* (pp. 103–119). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3640543.3645199

subtheme: A. Definition and dimensions of trust
relation: Definition and measure; supports measuring a single overall trust rating plus the three trustworthiness dimensions, since they are not interchangeable, and supports a direct trust item such as our 0 to 10 scale. Our study adds a time course within one encounter and an external source of doubt.
ref: Colquitt, J. A., Scott, B. A., & LePine, J. A. (2007). Trust, trustworthiness, and trust propensity: A meta-analytic test of their unique relationships with risk taking and job performance. *Journal of Applied Psychology*, *92*(4), 909–927. https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.92.4.909

subtheme: B. What a fact-check does to evaluation of the checked speaker
relation: Speaker evaluation; an exoneration analogue for H2: a false accusation hurts, and a credible rebuttal can restore standing. In our study the rebuttal comes from the accused CISO, not from a third party, which is a weaker source.
ref: Dan, V. (2025). Deepfakes as a democratic threat: Experimental evidence shows noxious effects that are reducible through journalistic fact checks. *The International Journal of Press/Politics*, *31*(3), 525–550. https://doi.org/10.1177/19401612251317766

subtheme: C. Checkers in the listener's hand: wearable and interactive reasoning aids
access: open access https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00024 (CHI version listed as open at https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713408)
relation: Sub-theme C; H1 and H4. Our flags are wrong but sound plausible ("right by the textbook"), which is close to this paper's deceptive explanations; we add the step where the human expert answers back.
ref: Danry, V., Pataranutaporn, P., Groh, M., & Epstein, Z. (2025). Deceptive explanations by large language models lead people to change their beliefs about misinformation more often than honest explanations. In *Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems* (pp. 1–31). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713408

subtheme: C. Wrong, partial or over-broad flags (implied truth, tainted truth)
type: other HCI (preprint, listed by the authors as accepted to ICWSM 2027)
relation: Wrong AI flags; supports H1 for content: a wrong AI verdict lowers trust in correct material by about a quarter of the scale. Extends Freeze et al. to LLM checkers. Our target is the person presenting, not a headline.
ref: He, J., Horne, B. D., & Nevo, D. (2026). *On the effectiveness of fact checking information from politically congruent and incongruent large language models* (arXiv:2607.15364) [Preprint]. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15364

subtheme: C. Trust repair after a competence or integrity question
access: open access repository record https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/lkcsb_research/2578 ; journal via SFU library
relation: H2; our reasoned answers ("the company's reason") are a kind of external, situational account for an apparent competence lapse. This paper predicts that external accounts help less for competence violations, a counterweight to H2. Our CISO is not admitting a lapse but explaining why the flag does not apply, which is closer to a justification than to an apology.
ref: Kim, P. H., Dirks, K. T., Cooper, C. D., & Ferrin, D. L. (2006). When more blame is better than less: The implications of internal vs. external attributions for the repair of trust after a competence- vs. integrity-based trust violation. *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes*, *99*(1), 49–65. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2005.07.002

subtheme: E. Continued influence, innuendo and belief echoes
relation: H1; a modern, preregistered anchor that a hedged, question-like flag is enough to lower trust in a person, even with no evidence. Our flags are hedged machine verdicts about an expert's slides, shown to the participant in a private panel.
ref: Letourneau, D., & Gawronski, B. (2024). Incrimination through innuendo: A replication and extension. *Social Psychology*, *55*(1), 51–61. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000540

subtheme: D. AI credibility flags, and flags that are wrong
relation: Sub-theme D; H1 and H4 (people align with a wrong AI; showing the flag before one's own judgement strengthens it, as in our design where the flag appears with the slide). Predecessor of the known Lu et al. CHI 2025 paper. Content only, no speaker.
ref: Lu, Z., Li, P., Wang, W., & Yin, M. (2022). The effects of AI-based credibility indicators on the detection and spread of misinformation under social influence. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *6*(CSCW2), 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1145/3555562

subtheme: Sub-theme C: Over-reliance, explanations, confidence and second opinions (SIGCHI)
relation: Second opinions; H2 and H4: the CISO's answer functions as a human second opinion against the checker, and asking for it is the "on demand" condition. Our study differs because the second opinion comes from the person under scrutiny, and we measure trust in that person.
ref: Lu, Z., Wang, D., & Yin, M. (2024). Does more advice help? The effects of second opinions in AI-assisted decision making. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *8*(CSCW1), 1–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/3653708

subtheme: A. Definition and dimensions of trust
relation: Definition and measure; a CISO briefing a board for one session is a case where cognition-based trust dominates, so our 0 to 10 rating and the competence item are measuring mostly cognition-based trust. Our study uses a short, one-off encounter, not an ongoing peer relationship.
ref: McAllister, D. J. (1995). Affect- and cognition-based trust as foundations for interpersonal cooperation in organizations. *Academy of Management Journal*, *38*(1), 24–59. https://doi.org/10.2307/256727

subtheme: Sub-theme A: Algorithm versus human advisor, and advice conflict (judge-advisor systems)
relation: Advice conflict; H2 and H3 context: an error is forgiven more readily in a human than in an algorithm, so a checker that is shown to be wrong (the CISO's reasoned answer) may lose more standing than the CISO. Our study measures the human's standing after the algorithm errs about the human, which this work does not.
ref: Prahl, A., & Van Swol, L. (2017). Understanding algorithm aversion: When is advice from automation discounted? *Journal of Forecasting*, *36*(6), 691–702. https://doi.org/10.1002/for.2464

subtheme: B. Industry and trade sources
access: Open access press release; full report free behind a form. Accessed 2026-10-18.
relation: Context. A third of board members and CISOs report misalignment, so the relationship is not secure and a flag could tip it. It is a vendor survey, so these are self-reports from a commercial source.
ref: Proofpoint. (2023). *Cybersecurity: The 2023 board perspective*. Proofpoint. https://www.proofpoint.com/us/newsroom/press-releases/proofpoints-second-annual-board-perspective-report-reveals-nearly-three-five

subtheme: C. Trust repair after a competence or integrity question
relation: Definition and measure for H2: our "restores trust, possibly above the start" needs exactly this distinction between partial repair, complete repair and over-repair, which requires a pre-violation baseline (our start rating) and a post-violation rating (our after-flag rating). It is the most recent review and replaces the older Kramer and Lewicki (2010) and Lewicki and Brinsfield (2017) reviews for our purposes.
ref: Sharma, K., Schoorman, F. D., & Ballinger, G. A. (2023). How can it be made right again? A review of trust repair research. *Journal of Management*, *49*(1), 363–399. https://doi.org/10.1177/01492063221089897

subtheme: D. Explanations and accounts
relation: H2 and H3; explanation versus no explanation is our reasoned answer versus denial contrast. Our reasoned answers are justifications ("this is right for our company"), which this meta-analysis finds less effective than excuses, a point worth stating. Our outcome is trust in an expert, not fairness of a decision.
ref: Shaw, J. C., Wild, E., & Colquitt, J. A. (2003). To justify or excuse?: A meta-analytic review of the effects of explanations. *Journal of Applied Psychology*, *88*(3), 444–458. https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.88.3.444

subtheme: A. Anchors: what fact-checks do on average, and what persists
relation: Speaker evaluation after a correction; grounds H1 and the limit of H2: a flag that is later answered may still leave a residue on trust in the CISO. Our flag is wrong and the answer comes from the flagged person, not from a third party.
ref: Thorson, E. (2016). Belief echoes: The persistent effects of corrected misinformation. *Political Communication*, *33*(3), 460–480. https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2015.1102187

subtheme: Sub-theme B: Disclosed AI use lowers trust in the professional
relation: use penalty; measure (warmth and competence as mediators of interpersonal trust). Weak design for our purposes; include only if space allows.
ref: Zhang, Z., Geng, J., & Qi, C. (2026). Observer perceptions of GenAI use and interpersonal trust: The roles of warmth, competence, and AI literacy. *Behavioral Sciences*, *16*(7), Article 1221. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071221

subtheme: B. What a fact-check does to evaluation of the checked speaker
relation: Speaker evaluation; counter-result to H1 in a high-stakes field setting. Our participant is a decision maker who must act (the budget), which may make trust more sensitive to flags than voting support is.
ref: Barrera, O., Guriev, S., Henry, E., & Zhuravskaya, E. (2020). Facts, alternative facts, and fact checking in times of post-truth politics. *Journal of Public Economics*, *182*, 104123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2019.104123

subtheme: C. Checkers in the listener's hand: wearable and interactive reasoning aids
relation: Sub-theme C; design element. A checker that asks instead of asserting ("Do the numbers add up?") is a design alternative to our assertive flags; relevant to H4, since question framing may push the board member to ask the CISO rather than to challenge.
ref: Danry, V., Pataranutaporn, P., Mao, Y., & Maes, P. (2023). Don't just tell me, ask me: AI systems that intelligently frame explanations as questions improve human logical discernment accuracy over causal AI explanations. In *Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems* (pp. 1–13). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3580672

subtheme: C. Products: camera assistants, meeting assistants and live fact-checkers
relation: Product context. These show the live fact-checker as a working genre. Our checker differs in three ways: it reads visual slides, it sits with a single audience member, and it judges a colleague in a private, high-stakes setting rather than a public politician.
ref: Full Fact AI (since 2016) and Factiverse (live debate fact-checking, 2024)

subtheme: A. Board-level cybersecurity governance and the CISO-board relationship (scholarly)
relation: Context. It shows that directors lack the knowledge to evaluate cyber reports and lean on whoever holds it. The checker in our study could take the place of the "one cyber-literate member". Gale et al. describe governance structures; we measure individual trust.
ref: Gale, M., Bongiovanni, I., & Slapničar, S. (2022). Governing cybersecurity from the boardroom: Challenges, drivers, and ways ahead. *Computers & Security*, *121*, Article 102840. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cose.2022.102840

subtheme: Sub-theme E: Trust in automation and in AI: definitions, models and measurement
relation: Definition and theme anchor for trust in the checker (embedded AI, cognitive trust); management venue suits the board framing. Gap: the review covers trust in AI, not how AI shapes trust between people.
ref: Glikson, E., & Woolley, A. W. (2020). Human trust in artificial intelligence: Review of empirical research. *Academy of Management Annals*, *14*(2), 627–660. https://doi.org/10.5465/annals.2018.0057

subtheme: A. AI-mediated communication: AI involvement changes how a person is judged
type: communication (core reference for HCI AI-MC work)
access: SFU library (Oxford Academic, may be free on the publisher page)
relation: Sub-theme A; definition. Our checker is a variant the definition does not cover: the agent acts for the *receiver* (the board member) and comments on the sender's message instead of producing it. One sentence for the review: we extend AI-MC from sender-side to receiver-side mediation.
ref: Hancock, J. T., Naaman, M., & Levy, K. (2020). AI-mediated communication: Definition, research agenda, and ethical considerations. *Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication*, *25*(1), 89–100. https://doi.org/10.1093/jcmc/zmz022

subtheme: Sub-theme B: Automation bias and wrong AI advice
relation: Design element and gap: our checker's flags are wrong precisely because of unobservables (the company's context only the CISO knows). The CISO's reasoned answer is in effect a disclosure of unobservables; this paper shows that telling people about them does not guarantee they use them well. We test this socially, with the unobservable voiced by the flagged human.
ref: Holstein, K., De-Arteaga, M., Tumati, L., & Cheng, Y. (2023). Toward supporting perceptual complementarity in human-AI collaboration via reflection on unobservables. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *7*(CSCW1), 1–20. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579628

subtheme: D. AI credibility flags, and flags that are wrong
relation: Sub-theme D; supports H1 (an AI-sourced warning is at least as persuasive as a human one) and suggests a moderator (prior institutional trust). Target is content, not a speaker.
ref: Horne, B. D. (2025). Does the source of a warning matter? Examining the effectiveness of veracity warning labels across warners. *Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media*, *19*, 823–836. https://doi.org/10.1609/icwsm.v19i1.35848

subtheme: Sub-theme D: Large language models that are confidently wrong
relation: Design element for the checker's wording ("Architecture likely wrong" is a hedged, impersonal verdict). Predicts that a stronger or weaker hedge will change how much the flag moves trust (H1). Our study measures trust in the flagged human.
ref: Kim, S. S. Y., Liao, Q. V., Vorvoreanu, M., Ballard, S., & Vaughan, J. W. (2024). "I'm not sure, but...": Examining the impact of large language models' uncertainty expression on user reliance and trust. In *Proceedings of the 2024 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency* (pp. 822–835). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3630106.3658941

subtheme: Sub-theme E: Trust in automation and in AI: definitions, models and measurement
relation: Definition of appropriate reliance and calibration. Our study runs the transfer the other way: trust in automation shaping trust in a person.
ref: Lee, J. D., & See, K. A. (2004). Trust in automation: Designing for appropriate reliance. *Human Factors*, *46*(1), 50–80. https://doi.org/10.1518/hfes.46.1.50_30392

subtheme: F. AI as challenger or second opinion in groups, and power
relation: Sub-theme F; context for how a second opinion shifts reliance between two sources. Here the AI is the primary advisor and the human the second opinion; our study reverses this (human expert first, AI checker second) and measures trust in the human.
ref: Lu, Z., Wang, D., & Yin, M. (2024). Does more advice help? The effects of second opinions in AI-assisted decision making. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *8*(CSCW1), 1–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/3653708

subtheme: C. Checkers in the listener's hand: wearable and interactive reasoning aids
relation: Sub-theme C; H1 and H4 (users follow a wrong checker), and a design precedent for a UIST-style checker. Claims had no human speaker who could answer back, which is what our design adds.
ref: Nguyen, A. T., Kharosekar, A., Krishnan, S., Krishnan, S., Tate, E., Wallace, B. C., & Lease, M. (2018). Believe it or not: Designing a human-AI partnership for mixed-initiative fact-checking. In *Proceedings of the 31st Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology* (pp. 189–199). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3242587.3242666

subtheme: D. AI credibility flags, and flags that are wrong
relation: Sub-theme D; counter-result to the machine heuristic: an automated label can be less trusted than a human fact-check, which bears on how much weight a board member gives the checker in H1.
ref: Seo, H., Xiong, A., & Lee, D. (2019). Trust it or not: Effects of machine-learning warnings in helping individuals mitigate misinformation. In *Proceedings of the 10th ACM Conference on Web Science* (pp. 265–274). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3292522.3326012

subtheme: C. Trust repair after a competence or integrity question
relation: H2 and H3, mechanism; a reasoned answer works if it moves the cause of the flagged problem away from the CISO's ability (for example, a company-specific constraint), while a bare denial leaves the attribution unchanged. Our study tests this in a live exchange where the "negative outcome" is an AI flag, not an actual loss.
ref: Tomlinson, E. C., & Mayer, R. C. (2009). The role of causal attribution dimensions in trust repair. *Academy of Management Review*, *34*(1), 85–104. https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2009.35713291

subtheme: Sub-theme E: Trust in automation and in AI: definitions, models and measurement
relation: Measure: guides our trust measurement (state the definition, separate trust from reliance, measure before and after). Supports measuring trust in the CISO as competence, benevolence and integrity rather than a single item alone.
ref: Vereschak, O., Bailly, G., & Caramiaux, B. (2021). How to evaluate trust in AI-assisted decision making? A survey of empirical methodologies. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *5*(CSCW2), 1–39. https://doi.org/10.1145/3476068

subtheme: A. Anchors: what fact-checks do on average, and what persists
relation: Anchor for the corrections literature. Shows the outcome studied is belief in the claim, not trust in the speaker. Our study measures trust in the person who is flagged, and the flag is wrong, which this literature does not cover.
ref: Walter, N., Cohen, J., Holbert, R. L., & Morag, Y. (2020). Fact-checking: A meta-analysis of what works and for whom. *Political Communication*, *37*(3), 350–375. https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2019.1668894

subtheme: E. Continued influence, innuendo and belief echoes
relation: H1 and H3; our flags ("Architecture likely wrong") are hedged, like innuendo, and the result that source credibility matters little for innuendo predicts that even a doubted AI checker will lower trust. The denial result predicts that the CISO's bare denial can itself repeat the charge. Our target is an expert present in the exchange, and the innuendo comes from an AI tool.
ref: Wegner, D. M., Wenzlaff, R., Kerker, R. M., & Beattie, A. E. (1981). Incrimination through innuendo: Can media questions become public answers? *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, *40*(5), 822–832. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.40.5.822

subtheme: Sub-theme C: Over-reliance, explanations, confidence and second opinions (SIGCHI)
relation: Trust calibration definition; design element (our flags carry "likely", a verbal confidence cue). The "unique knowledge" condition maps onto the CISO, not the board member, which is what makes our setting different: the knowledge that corrects the AI sits with the person being flagged.
ref: Zhang, Y., Liao, Q. V., & Bellamy, R. K. E. (2020). Effect of confidence and explanation on accuracy and trust calibration in AI-assisted decision making. In *Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency* (pp. 295–305). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3351095.3372852

subtheme: F. AI as challenger or second opinion in groups, and power
relation: Sub-theme F; H4 (amplification). An outside example that the social setting can magnify both good and bad responses to the same AI input, as H4 predicts for the checker group. No human target is evaluated.
ref: de Brito Duarte, R., Abreu, M. C., Campos, J., & Paiva, A. (2025). The amplifying effect of explainability in AI-assisted decision-making in groups. In *Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems* (pp. 1–15). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713534

subtheme: Sub-theme C: Over-reliance, explanations, confidence and second opinions (SIGCHI)
relation: Over-reliance; H1 and H4: a flag with a stated reason ("Numbers do not add up") should be accepted more readily even when wrong. Our checker flags a person in a social setting, not a classification label.
ref: Bansal, G., Wu, T., Zhou, J., Fok, R., Nushi, B., Kamar, E., Ribeiro, M. T., & Weld, D. (2021). Does the whole exceed its parts? The effect of AI explanations on complementary team performance. In *Proceedings of the 2021 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems* (pp. 1–16). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3411764.3445717

subtheme: D. Explanations and accounts
relation: H2 and H3; an account must be judged adequate to help, which supports giving the CISO a concrete company reason (two answers) against a bare denial (one answer). Our outcome is trust in an expert after an AI flag rather than fairness after a managerial decision.
ref: Bies, R. J., & Shapiro, D. L. (1987). Interactional fairness judgments: The influence of causal accounts. *Social Justice Research*, *1*(2), 199–218. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01048016

subtheme: Sub-theme C: Over-reliance, explanations, confidence and second opinions (SIGCHI)
relation: Over-reliance and dual-process account; H4 design element: our trust rating before the CISO answers and the forced choice (nothing, explain, challenge) work like a cognitive forcing step. Need for Cognition is a candidate covariate. Our study measures trust in the human, not decision accuracy.
ref: Buçinca, Z., Malaya, M. B., & Gajos, K. Z. (2021). To trust or to think: Cognitive forcing functions can reduce overreliance on AI in AI-assisted decision-making. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *5*(CSCW1), 1–21. https://doi.org/10.1145/3449287

subtheme: D. AI-labelled checkers and how a checked human is judged
relation: Flag format; our flags are short verdicts ("Numbers do not add up") without reasons, the format this study found least trusted. Also parallels H2 and H3: a reason is what makes a claim trusted, for checker and for CISO alike.
ref: Drolsbach, C. P., Solovev, K., & Pröllochs, N. (2024). Community notes increase trust in fact-checking on social media. *PNAS Nexus*, *3*(7), pgae217. https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae217

subtheme: E. Continued influence, innuendo and belief echoes
relation: H2 counter-result and theme anchor for continued influence; together with Thorson (2016) it predicts residual trust loss after a good answer. It replaces Lewandowsky et al. (2012) as the up-to-date citation. Our "misinformation" is an AI flag about a person's work, not a factual claim about the world.
ref: Ecker, U. K. H., Lewandowsky, S., Cook, J., Schmid, P., Fazio, L. K., Brashier, N., Kendeou, P., Vraga, E. K., & Amazeen, M. A. (2022). The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction. *Nature Reviews Psychology*, *1*(1), 13–29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-021-00006-y

subtheme: C. Wrong, partial or over-broad flags (implied truth, tainted truth)
relation: Wrong flags; the direct precedent for our design, where every flag is wrong. Supports H1 (a wrong flag still costs credibility). The target here is a news story, not a person who can answer back.
ref: Freeze, M., Baumgartner, M., Bruno, P., Gunderson, J. R., Olin, J., Ross, M. Q., & Szafran, J. (2021). Fake claims of fake news: Political misinformation, warnings, and the tainted truth effect. *Political Behavior*, *43*(4), 1433–1465. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11109-020-09597-3

subtheme: C. Products: camera assistants, meeting assistants and live fact-checkers
relation: Product. This is the canonical live claim spotter and the filter inside Squash. It decides what to check but gives no verdict tied to the speaker's context. No audience trust outcomes.
ref: Hassan, N., Arslan, F., Li, C., & Tremayne, M. (2017). Toward automated fact-checking: Detecting check-worthy factual claims by ClaimBuster. In *Proceedings of the 23rd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining* (pp. 1803–1812). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3098131

subtheme: Sub-theme D: Large language models that are confidently wrong
relation: H1 and H2: a flag with a reason attached will be accepted even when wrong; a counter-account that exposes an inconsistency (the CISO naming the company context) is the kind of cue that lowers reliance on the wrong answer. Our flags have no sources, by design.
ref: Kim, S. S. Y., Vaughan, J. W., Liao, Q. V., Lombrozo, T., & Russakovsky, O. (2025). Fostering appropriate reliance on large language models: The role of explanations, sources, and inconsistencies. In *Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems* (pp. 1–19). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3714020

subtheme: Sub-theme C: Over-reliance, explanations, confidence and second opinions (SIGCHI)
relation: Theme anchor and gap: the surveyed designs have a human deciding with AI help; none in the abstract involve the AI assessing another human. Lets us state that our human-AI-human design falls outside the mapped design space.
ref: Lai, V., Chen, C., Smith-Renner, A., Liao, Q. V., & Tan, C. (2023). Towards a science of human-AI decision making: An overview of design space in empirical human-subject studies. In *Proceedings of the 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency* (pp. 1369–1385). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3593013.3594087

subtheme: D. Reliability of vision-language models and LLM fact-checkers
relation: VLM reliability, as a counter-result. LLMs do detect textbook chart problems, which makes our checker's flags plausible ("right by the textbook"). Lo is a co-author of the known paper Lo et al. (2022). Together with Bendeck & Stasko this frames the checker as good at rule-based critique and blind to company context.
ref: Lo, L. Y.-H., & Qu, H. (2025). How good (or bad) are LLMs at detecting misleading visualizations? *IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics*, *31*(1), 1116–1125. https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2024.3456333

subtheme: A. AI-mediated communication: AI involvement changes how a person is judged
relation: Sub-theme A; context for H1 (an AI in the channel can lower interpersonal perception even when it is not aimed at the person). Our study differs because the AI openly contradicts the speaker instead of quietly shaping their words.
ref: Mieczkowski, H., Hancock, J. T., Naaman, M., Jung, M., & Hohenstein, J. (2021). AI-mediated communication: Language use and interpersonal effects in a referential communication task. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *5*(CSCW1), 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3449091

subtheme: C. Wrong, partial or over-broad flags (implied truth, tainted truth)
relation: Wrong or partial flags; design element: our checker says "No issues found" on slides 1 and 5, which is an explicit verification and so may raise trust on those slides by contrast. Supports interpreting the flag pattern as a whole, not slide by slide.
ref: Pennycook, G., Bear, A., Collins, E. T., & Rand, D. G. (2020). The implied truth effect: Attaching warnings to a subset of fake news headlines increases perceived accuracy of headlines without warnings. *Management Science*, *66*(11), 4944–4957. https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2019.3478

subtheme: A. Definition and dimensions of trust
relation: Definition (the most quoted one, also used by Sharma et al. 2023 to define trust repair). The board member accepts vulnerability to the CISO's expertise; the checker offers a partial substitute for that vulnerability. Our study measures how the state moves within a ten-minute exchange.
ref: Rousseau, D. M., Sitkin, S. B., Burt, R. S., & Camerer, C. (1998). Not so different after all: A cross-discipline view of trust. *Academy of Management Review*, *23*(3), 393–404. https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.1998.926617

subtheme: Sub-theme D: Large language models that are confidently wrong
relation: Calibration; H1 and H4: people over-trust fluent model output, which supports a drop in trust in the CISO after a flag. Our checker gives terse verdicts, which this work suggests may be trusted less than long ones.
ref: Steyvers, M., Tejeda, H., Kumar, A., Belem, C., Karny, S., Hu, X., Mayer, L. W., & Smyth, P. (2025). What large language models know and what people think they know. *Nature Machine Intelligence*, *7*(2), 221–231. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-024-00976-7

subtheme: B. Machine heuristic: why a checker's verdict carries weight
relation: Sub-theme B; theory anchor for H1 and H4: a non-expert may give an automated flag more weight than a human expert's word. Our study tests this in the reverse direction (machine against human).
ref: Sundar, S. S., & Kim, J. (2019). Machine heuristic: When we trust computers more than humans with our personal information. In *Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems* (pp. 1–9). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3290605.3300768

subtheme: B. Machine heuristic: why a checker's verdict carries weight
relation: Sub-theme B; measure. A short pre-study covariate that could explain who follows the checker (H4 amplification). Not a trust-in-person study.
ref: Yang, H., & Sundar, S. S. (2024). Machine heuristic: Concept explication and development of a measurement scale. *Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication*, *29*(6), Article zmae019. https://doi.org/10.1093/jcmc/zmae019

subtheme: Sub-theme A: Algorithm versus human advisor, and advice conflict (judge-advisor systems)
relation: Advice conflict; H4 measure context: how the checker is described will drive how much its flag weighs, and our board judgements (is this architecture right for this company) are the subjective, uncertain kind where advice weighs most. Weight on advice is a behaviour measure; we measure trust in the human advisor.
ref: Bailey, P. E., Leon, T., Ebner, N. C., Moustafa, A. A., & Weidemann, G. (2023). A meta-analysis of the weight of advice in decision-making. *Current Psychology*, *42*(28), 24516–24541. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-022-03573-2

subtheme: D. Reliability of vision-language models and LLM fact-checkers
relation: VLM reliability. Language hallucination is the mechanism behind "right by the textbook, wrong for this company": the model answers from what is usually true rather than from what the slide shows in context.
ref: Guan, T., Liu, F., Wu, X., Xian, R., Li, Z., Liu, X., Wang, X., Chen, L., Huang, F., Yacoob, Y., Manocha, D., & Zhou, T. (2024). HallusionBench: An advanced diagnostic suite for entangled language hallucination and visual illusion in large vision-language models. In *Proceedings of the 2024 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)* (pp. 14375–14385). IEEE. https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52733.2024.01363

subtheme: A. Board-level cybersecurity governance and the CISO-board relationship (scholarly)
relation: Context, supporting H2. CISO standing with the board depends on communication. This is an early source the brief expected. Its evidence base is thin compared with Proudfoot et al. (2023).
ref: Hooper, V., & McKissack, J. (2016). The emerging role of the CISO. *Business Horizons*, *59*(6), 585–591. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bushor.2016.07.004

subtheme: D. Reliability of vision-language models and LLM fact-checkers
type: other (machine learning benchmark, NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks)
relation: VLM reliability on documents. Even the best models fail on most questions about multi-page business-style documents. A checker that sees one slide at a time also lacks the cross-page context, which is how our flags go wrong.
ref: Ma, Y., Zang, Y., Chen, L., Chen, M., Jiao, Y., Li, X., Lu, X., Liu, Z., Ma, Y., Dong, X., Zhang, P., Pan, L., Jiang, Y.-G., Wang, J., Cao, Y., & Sun, A. (2024). MMLongBench-Doc: Benchmarking long-context document understanding with visualizations. In *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37* (pp. 95963–96010). Curran Associates. https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-3041

subtheme: E. The checked party's response and behaviour
relation: Behaviour of the checked party; a failed conceptual replication of the known Nyhan and Reifler deterrence effect. Context for the "checked person adapts" thread; our CISO's behaviour is scripted, so this is background only.
ref: Ma, S., Bergan, D., Ahn, S., Carnahan, D., Gimby, N., McGraw, J., & Virtue, I. (2023). Fact-checking as a deterrent? A conceptual replication of the influence of fact-checking on the sharing of misinformation by political elites. *Human Communication Research*, *49*(3), 321–338. https://doi.org/10.1093/hcr/hqac031

subtheme: B. Industry and trade sources
short: National Association of Corporate Directors & Internet Security Alliance. (2023)
access: Free digital version with NACD registration. Accessed 2026-10-18.
relation: Context and design element. The professional norm is that directors should question the CISO. Our "ask the CISO to explain" and "challenge" options turn that norm into an action participants can take. The handbook's question lists are a human-authored alternative to an AI checker.
ref: National Association of Corporate Directors & Internet Security Alliance. (2023). *Director's handbook on cyber-risk oversight* (4th ed.). NACD. https://www.nacdonline.org/all-governance/governance-resources/trending-oversight-topics/cybersecurity/

subtheme: D. Reliability of vision-language models and LLM fact-checkers
relation: VLM reliability. Architecture diagrams with overlapping boxes and lines (our slide 2, "Architecture likely wrong") are exactly where VLMs fail. This supports the plausibility of a wrong architecture flag.
ref: Rahmanzadehgervi, P., Bolton, L., Taesiri, M. R., & Nguyen, A. T. (2024). Vision language models are blind. In *Computer Vision – ACCV 2024* (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, pp. 293–309). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-96-0917-8_17

subtheme: Sub-theme C: Over-reliance, explanations, confidence and second opinions (SIGCHI)
relation: Over-reliance as a cost-benefit choice; H4: board members who cannot verify a slide cheaply will lean on the flag; asking the CISO is a low-cost verification route, which our "ask to explain" option offers. We measure trust in the human after verification, not agreement with the AI.
ref: Vasconcelos, H., Jörke, M., Grunde-McLaughlin, M., Gerstenberg, T., Bernstein, M. S., & Krishna, R. (2023). Explanations can reduce overreliance on AI systems during decision-making. *Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction*, *7*(CSCW1), 1–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579605

subtheme: D. Reliability of vision-language models and LLM fact-checkers
relation: VLM reliability. On realistic charts, the best model gets more than half of the reasoning questions wrong. This is a citable error rate for "a VLM reading a slide chart is often wrong".
ref: Wang, Z., Xia, M., He, L., Chen, H., Liu, Y., Zhu, R., Liang, K., Wu, X., Liu, H., Malladi, S., Chevalier, A., Arora, S., & Chen, D. (2024). CharXiv: Charting gaps in realistic chart understanding in multimodal LLMs. In *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37* (pp. 113569–113697). Curran Associates. https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-3609

subtheme: C. Products: camera assistants, meeting assistants and live fact-checkers
relation: Product and design contrast. Community Notes shows a verdict only after agreement across viewpoints. Our checker gives a single machine verdict with no such safeguard and no context from the speaker. The two make a useful contrast for the discussion.
ref: Wojcik, S., Hilgard, S., Judd, N., Mocanu, D., Ragain, S., Hunzaker, M. B. F., Coleman, K., & Baxter, J. (2022). *Birdwatch: Crowd wisdom and bridging algorithms can inform understanding and reduce the spread of misinformation* (arXiv:2210.15723). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2210.15723

subtheme: Sub-theme A: Algorithm versus human advisor, and advice conflict (judge-advisor systems)
relation: Definition and theme anchor: the board member is a judge, the CISO and the checker are two advisors who disagree. The JAS literature measures weight on advice, not trust in the advisor, which is the gap our trust ratings fill.
ref: Bonaccio, S., & Dalal, R. S. (2006). Advice taking and decision-making: An integrative literature review, and implications for the organizational sciences. *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes*, *101*(2), 127–151. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.07.001

subtheme: C. Wrong, partial or over-broad flags (implied truth, tainted truth)
relation: Wrong or over-broad flags; supports the idea that the mere presence of a checker can make people doubt correct content, which bears on H4 (checker group more sceptical overall). Our study measures trust in a person, not accuracy ratings of headlines.
ref: Clayton, K., Blair, S., Busam, J. A., Forstner, S., Glance, J., Green, G., Kawata, A., Kovvuri, A., Martin, J., Morgan, E., Sandhu, M., Sang, R., Scholz-Bright, R., Welch, A. T., Wolff, A. G., Zhou, A., & Nyhan, B. (2020). Real solutions for fake news? Measuring the effectiveness of general warnings and fact-check tags in reducing belief in false stories on social media. *Political Behavior*, *42*(4), 1073–1095. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11109-019-09533-0

subtheme: E. Continued influence, innuendo and belief echoes
relation: Source credibility anchor and H2 counter-result; even if the board member learns the checker was wrong, the flag's content may outlive the memory that it came from a discredited source. Our study measures trust minutes after the flag, before any sleeper effect, which is a limit to state.
ref: Hovland, C. I., & Weiss, W. (1951). The influence of source credibility on communication effectiveness. *Public Opinion Quarterly*, *15*(4), 635–650. https://doi.org/10.1086/266350

subtheme: B. Industry and trade sources
relation: Context. Boards now own cyber risk, but they place accountability for it on the CISO. That is the expert on whom the board depends in our scenario.

subtheme: A. Board-level cybersecurity governance and the CISO-board relationship (scholarly)
relation: Context only (agency framing of CISO and principals). Marginal for H1 to H4. Included because the brief names it and markers may expect it.

access: HBR paywall (SFU library via HBR in Business Source Complete). Accessed 2026-10-18.
